questions.questionText: Which estimate is most reasonable for the height of point P?
questions.correctAnswer: About 225 m
questions.explanation: P lies between the 200 m and 250 m contours, so about 225 m is reasonable.

curriculum.objective: Use scale, contours and sampling methods to interpret places and collect representative evidence.

questions.questionText: What real distance does the mapped 6 cm route represent?
questions.correctAnswer: 15 km
questions.explanation: At 2.5 km per centimetre, 6 cm represents 6 × 2.5 = 15 km.

curriculum.objective: Use scale, contours and sampling methods to interpret places and collect representative evidence.

questions.questionText: Why might a fieldwork team use systematic sampling along a transect?
options: To select only the most dramatic locations
To guarantee every site is identical
To collect observations at regular, repeatable intervals
To avoid recording the sampling method
questions.correctAnswer: To collect observations at regular, repeatable intervals
questions.explanation: Regular intervals reduce arbitrary site choice and make the method repeatable.

curriculum.objective: Use scale, contours and sampling methods to interpret places and collect representative evidence.

questions.questionText: Students survey noise only beside the busiest road at lunchtime. What is the main limitation?
options: Lunch provides too many map coordinates
The sample does not represent other places or times
questions.correctAnswer: The sample does not represent other places or times
questions.explanation: One busy location and one time create spatial and temporal sampling bias.

curriculum.objective: Use scale, contours and sampling methods to interpret places and collect representative evidence.

questions.questionText: Which months form the main wet season in the climate graph?
questions.correctAnswer: June to August
questions.explanation: The rainfall bars are consistently tallest during June, July and August.

curriculum.objective: Interpret climate evidence and explain atmospheric and water-cycle processes across places.

questions.questionText: What process changes surface water into water vapour?
questions.correctAnswer: Evaporation
questions.explanation: Solar energy enables liquid water at the surface to become water vapour.

curriculum.objective: Interpret climate evidence and explain atmospheric and water-cycle processes across places.

questions.questionText: Why is a city centre often warmer than nearby countryside at night?
options: Cities receive more hours of sunlight
Buildings store heat and release it slowly
Wind can never enter a city
questions.correctAnswer: Buildings store heat and release it slowly
questions.explanation: Urban materials absorb daytime energy and release it slowly, contributing to a heat island.

curriculum.objective: Interpret climate evidence and explain atmospheric and water-cycle processes across places.

questions.questionText: A climate graph uses averages from only two years. Why is its climate claim weak?
options: Climate patterns require a much longer record
questions.correctAnswer: Climate patterns require a much longer record
questions.explanation: Two years may reflect short-term variability rather than a robust long-term climate pattern.

curriculum.objective: Interpret climate evidence and explain atmospheric and water-cycle processes across places.

questions.questionText: Where is the steepest gradient on the river profile?
questions.correctAnswer: Near the source
questions.explanation: The profile falls most rapidly over distance in the upper course near the source.

curriculum.objective: Explain how erosion, transport and deposition shape river and coastal landscapes and hazards.

questions.questionText: When is a river most likely to deposit sediment?
options: When it loses velocity and energy
questions.correctAnswer: When it loses velocity and energy
questions.explanation: A slower river has less capacity and competence, so it deposits part of its load.

curriculum.objective: Explain how erosion, transport and deposition shape river and coastal landscapes and hazards.

questions.questionText: How does hydraulic action erode a cliff?
options: Wind carries the entire cliff away
Waves compress air in cracks and weaken rock
Plants turn the rock into seawater
questions.correctAnswer: Waves compress air in cracks and weaken rock
questions.explanation: Repeated compression and release of trapped air widens cracks in the cliff.

curriculum.objective: Explain how erosion, transport and deposition shape river and coastal landscapes and hazards.

questions.questionText: A sea wall protects one town but increases erosion farther along the coast. Which process best explains this?
options: The wall increases global sea level
Reduced sediment supply interrupts longshore drift
questions.correctAnswer: Reduced sediment supply interrupts longshore drift
questions.explanation: Trapping sediment can starve downdrift beaches, reducing their protective width.

curriculum.objective: Explain how erosion, transport and deposition shape river and coastal landscapes and hazards.

questions.questionText: What dominant migration pattern is shown on the map?
options: Movement from rural settlements toward the city
Movement only from the city to villages
questions.correctAnswer: Movement from rural settlements toward the city
questions.explanation: The largest and most numerous arrows point from rural settlements into the city.

curriculum.objective: Analyse migration, population distribution and urban change using spatial and demographic evidence.

questions.questionText: Which is a likely pull factor for migration to a city?
options: Crop failure in a rural area
Greater access to jobs and services
questions.correctAnswer: Greater access to jobs and services
questions.explanation: Employment and service opportunities can attract people toward urban areas.

curriculum.objective: Analyse migration, population distribution and urban change using spatial and demographic evidence.

questions.questionText: A district has 84,000 people in 420 km². What is its population density?
questions.correctAnswer: 200 people per km²
questions.explanation: Population density is 84,000 ÷ 420 = 200 people per square kilometre.

curriculum.objective: Analyse migration, population distribution and urban change using spatial and demographic evidence.

questions.questionText: Why can rapid urbanisation create informal settlements?
options: All new residents prefer unsafe housing
Cities immediately run out of land everywhere
Urban jobs always disappear during growth
Housing and infrastructure may not grow as fast as population
questions.correctAnswer: Housing and infrastructure may not grow as fast as population
questions.explanation: When planned supply lags population growth, households may rely on unplanned housing.

curriculum.objective: Analyse migration, population distribution and urban change using spatial and demographic evidence.

questions.questionText: Which wind-farm site best balances strong wind with distance from homes and the nesting zone?
questions.correctAnswer: Site B
questions.explanation: B is exposed to the prevailing wind while lying away from both mapped constraints.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate resource and development decisions using environmental, social and economic evidence.

questions.questionText: Which energy source is renewable?
questions.correctAnswer: Solar radiation
questions.explanation: Sunlight is continually replenished on human timescales, unlike the finite fuels listed.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate resource and development decisions using environmental, social and economic evidence.

questions.questionText: Why is water described as renewable but still scarce in some places?
options: Earth creates unlimited clean water everywhere
Renewable means no management is needed
Supply varies by season, location, quality and demand
questions.correctAnswer: Supply varies by season, location, quality and demand
questions.explanation: The global cycle renews water, but accessible clean supply is uneven and demand can exceed it.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate resource and development decisions using environmental, social and economic evidence.

questions.questionText: Which proposal best demonstrates sustainable resource planning?
options: Maximise extraction this year regardless of damage
Ban all resource use without assessing needs
Judge success only by short-term profit
Meet present needs while protecting ecosystems and future supply
questions.correctAnswer: Meet present needs while protecting ecosystems and future supply
questions.explanation: Sustainability balances current social and economic needs with long-term environmental limits.

curriculum.objective: Evaluate resource and development decisions using environmental, social and economic evidence.
